title: Craig Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Craig wells have a 218 ft median depth, 9 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $16,900-$28,400.
h1: What Craig, Colorado Wells Are Like
intro_html:
This page covers permitted wells within 5 miles of Craig in Moffat County. The records show a wide range of conditions: 1,305 wells appear in Colorado DWR permit records, while 810 are recorded as constructed. Of those, 826 report total depth, 150 report pump yield, and 46 report a static water level.

Craig is not a place where one nearby well answers every question. Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, but 52 wells are listed in alluvial aquifers and 8 in the Mesa Verde. Use the local numbers to set expectations, then confirm the specific lot with neighboring well records, a driller, and the county or DWR before you buy or build.

sections.heading: Craig Well Depths Vary More Than a Typical Bid Suggests
sections.html:
The median permitted well near Craig is 218 feet deep. The middle half runs from 26 to 374 feet, so half of the reported wells fall across a very broad range. The 90th percentile is 484 feet, and the deepest record reaches 4,100 feet.

Depth mix helps explain why bids can differ. Thirty-eight percent of wells are under 100 feet, 23% are 100-300 feet, 34% are 300-600 feet, and 5% are 600 feet or deeper. A median-depth estimate is useful for budgeting, not a promise for a particular parcel. Mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground can change the drilling plan quickly, especially where permits identify fractured bedrock. Ask for a written price per foot and the added cost of casing, grout, pump work, and any extra drilling.

sections.heading: Most Craig Wells Produce a Usable Household Rate
sections.html:
Among the 150 Craig-area records that report pump yield, the median is 9.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 6.0 to 12.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-one percent fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 19% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

Ten percent are in the 1-5 gallon-per-minute range, while none of the reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute. That is encouraging for many household buyers, but it does not guarantee performance on an untested lot. Yield is not the same as storage in the well or water quality. Ask for the well construction report, pump test information, and any production limits before sizing a home, livestock use, irrigation system, or storage tank. An exempt household-use well still has Colorado use and pumping rules.

sections.heading: Craig Water Levels Look Fairly Stable by Decade
sections.html:
The reported median static water level near Craig is 77 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 8 to 124 feet. Only 46 records include a static water level, so this is a smaller sample than the depth data and should not be treated as a parcel-specific measurement.

The decade comparison does not show a dropping pattern in these records. The median was 80 feet below surface in the 2010s and 74 feet in the 2020s, meaning the later reported measurements were slightly shallower. That difference is not proof that water levels are rising across Craig; measurement dates, locations, pumping, and seasonal conditions matter. A buyer should locate the static level on the actual well record and have a driller check current conditions before finalizing a pump design.

sections.heading: Craig’s Permit History Shows Long-Term Drilling Activity
sections.html:
Craig has a long permit record, with permits issued from the 1950s through the 2020s. The largest decade was the 1990s with 261 permits. The record includes 181 from the 2000s, 185 from the 2010s, and 133 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2026.

The most active drillers named in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 175 wells; Visintainer Co. (Visintainer, Walter), with 69; and Craig Drilling (Herod, James Leroy), with 65. Those names show who appears often in the permit history, not who is available for your project or who should receive the work. Before relying on an older neighboring well, check its construction, pump, yield, and water-level documentation. Wells near Hayden, Maybell, and Meeker can provide regional context, but Craig-area records are more relevant to a Craig parcel.

sections.heading: A Craig Well at Median Depth May Cost $16,900-$28,400 Finished
sections.html:
For Craig’s mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, the cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $50-$75 per foot. At the 218-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $10,900-$16,400.

A finished system, including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, is estimated at $16,900-$28,400 at that median depth. The estimate changes if the hole must go substantially deeper, if access is difficult, or if the site needs more work than the model includes. Since the middle half of wells spans 26 to 374 feet, a bid based only on the median can understate the risk on a difficult parcel. Get the drilling rate, casing and grout terms, testing charges, pump package, trenching, electrical, and dry-hole terms in writing.

sections.heading: Craig Buyers Need to Check Water Quality and Site Constraints
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information deserves a closer look before purchase. Within about 10 miles of Craig, the records show 39 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 28 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These locations do not establish that a particular well is contaminated, but they are reasons to review maps, prior testing, and the proposed well location.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible even where nearby wells perform well, particularly with the large depth range and the predominance of unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer records. Septic design also needs adequate separation from the well and suitable soil and setbacks. Confirm the legal water use, DWR permit requirements, access for a rig, and the location of utilities before construction. If a property is in an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required for the intended use.

sections.heading: Before Buying or Building Near Craig, Verify the Specific Lot
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR records for the parcel and nearby wells. Compare reported depths, aquifers, construction details, yields, and static levels rather than relying on one neighbor. The local median yield of 9.0 gallons per minute is a useful planning figure, but only a minority of records report yield, so the data has limits.

For a purchase, make well condition, water testing, permit review, and a satisfactory inspection part of the contract. For a new build, have a driller evaluate access and likely depth before finalizing the house location. Coordinate the well, septic field, driveway, power trench, and building pad early. If you are comparing Craig with Hayden, Maybell, Oak Creek, Meeker, Clark, or Phippsburg, treat each area as its own groundwater setting and use the nearest relevant well records.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Craig, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth near Craig is 218 feet. The middle half ranges from 26 to 374 feet, while the 90th percentile is 484 feet. Thirty-eight percent are under 100 feet and 34% are 300-600 feet. That spread means a nearby well can help with planning, but it cannot guarantee the depth on your parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Craig?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50-$75 per foot. At the 218-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $10,900-$16,400. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $16,900-$28,400. A deeper hole, difficult access, or added site work can move the project outside those figures.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Craig?
faq.a: Among Craig-area records reporting pump yield, the median is 9.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 6.0-12.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-one percent report 5-15 gallons per minute, while 10% report 1-5. Pump yield is not a guarantee for a new well, so review the test and construction records for nearby wells.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Craig, Colorado?
faq.a: The well records do not establish that water from a specific Craig well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, mapped records include 39 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 28 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those findings call for site-specific testing and a review of nearby environmental records before relying on the water.

faq.q: Are Craig well water levels going down?
faq.a: The available records do not show a dropping trend. Median reported static water level was 80 feet below surface in the 2010s and 74 feet in the 2020s, compared with an overall median of 77 feet. Only 46 wells report a static water level, so these figures are regional indicators, not a current measurement for a particular property.
